1 Overview

This report estimates a reduced-form VAR for the Italian electricity market and identifies structural shocks via sign restrictions, following Kilian & Lütkepohl (2017, Ch. 13): Haar-uniform random rotations of the Cholesky factor (via QR decomposition), an admissible-set search over the configured sign restrictions, and Fry & Pagan (2011) median-target (MT) selection for the reported impulse responses. Confidence bands come from a frequentist residual bootstrap (Inoue & Kilian, 2013) that re-runs the entire identification search inside every replication.

Every modeling choice below (variables, transformations, lags, restrictions, bootstrap settings) is read from 00_config.R – that is the only file that needs editing to change the analysis.

1.1 Endogenous variables

var_table <- purrr::map_dfr(config$variables, ~ tibble::tibble(
  id = .x$id, file = .x$file, label = .x$label,
  transform = .x$transform, role = .x$role
))

2 Data loading

Each raw CSV is parsed with its own delimiter, date format, and decimal mark (per-variable settings in 00_config.R), then aligned onto one common monthly grid so any month missing from a source file surfaces as an explicit NA instead of silently shifting the other series out of alignment.

raw_data <- load_all_series(config)
cat(sprintf("Loaded %d monthly observations, %s to %s.\n",
            nrow(raw_data), min(raw_data$date), max(raw_data$date)))

## One look for every figure in this report: colours from grDevices'
## Okabe-Ito colourblind-safe palette, no plot box, horizontal tick labels,
## plain left-aligned titles, and a light horizontal grid behind the data.
## `theme_par(...)` takes the per-figure par settings (mfrow, mar) too, so
## each plotting chunk sets its layout and the style in one call.
pal <- grDevices::palette.colors(NULL, "Okabe-Ito")

theme_par <- function(...) {
  par(bty = "n", las = 1, tcl = -0.25, mgp = c(2.4, 0.5, 0), adj = 0,
      font.main = 1, cex.main = 1.05, col.main = "grey15",
      col.axis = "grey35", col.lab = "grey30", fg = "grey65", ...)
}

grid_h <- function() grid(nx = NA, ny = NULL, col = "grey92", lty = 1, lwd = 0.7)

#' Legend in the figure's top outer margin. The FEVD and historical
#' decomposition panels are filled edge to edge, so a legend placed inside any
#' one of them sits on the data. Pair with `oma = c(0, 0, 3, 0)` in the
#' theme_par() call so the outer margin exists to draw into.
top_legend <- function(...) {
  legend(grconvertX(0.5, "ndc", "user"), grconvertY(1, "ndc", "user"),
         xjust = 0.5, yjust = 1, xpd = NA,
         border = NA, bty = "n", cex = 0.85, ...)
}

#' Draw one plot into `plots_dir/<variable id>/<name>.png` instead of the
#' report -- the report shows the combined grids, the per-variable files are
#' for use outside it.
save_plot <- function(id, name, draw) {
  dir <- file.path(config$paths$plots_dir, id)
  dir.create(dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
  grDevices::png(file.path(dir, paste0(name, ".png")),
                 width = 7, height = 4.5, units = "in", res = 150)
  on.exit(grDevices::dev.off())
  theme_par(mar = c(3.5, 4, 3, 1))
  draw()
}

plot_series <- function(v) {
  plot(raw_data$date, raw_data[[v$id]], type = "l", col = pal[["blue"]], lwd = 1.5,
       xlab = "", ylab = "", main = v$label, panel.first = grid_h())
}

## NA-dropping matches the unit-root tests in 03_sanity_checks.R: the common
## monthly grid pads series that start late with explicit NAs.
plot_acf  <- function(v) stats::acf(stats::na.omit(raw_data[[v$id]]), lag.max = 36,
                                    main = paste("ACF:", v$label),
                                    col = pal[["blue"]], lwd = 1.5,
                                    ci.col = pal[["vermillion"]], panel.first = grid_h())
plot_pacf <- function(v) stats::pacf(stats::na.omit(raw_data[[v$id]]), lag.max = 36,
                                     main = paste("PACF:", v$label),
                                     col = pal[["blue"]], lwd = 1.5,
                                     ci.col = pal[["vermillion"]], panel.first = grid_h())
theme_par(mfrow = c(ceiling(length(config$variables) / 2), 2), mar = c(3, 4, 3, 1))
for (v in config$variables) plot_series(v)

for (v in config$variables) save_plot(v$id, "timeseries", function() plot_series(v))

2.1 Autocorrelation

Sample ACF and PACF of each raw series, over 36 monthly lags. The slow decay in the level series is what the transformations in 00_config.R address; spikes at lags 12, 24 and 36 (clearest in electricity consumption) are the calendar seasonality the monthly dummies absorb.

## Wider top/bottom margins than the raw-series grid: with 12 panels the
## default c(3, 4, 2, 1) leaves too little room and each panel title lands on
## the "Lag" axis of the panel above it.
theme_par(mfrow = c(length(config$variables), 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
for (v in config$variables) {
  plot_acf(v)
  plot_pacf(v)
}

for (v in config$variables) {
  save_plot(v$id, "acf", function() plot_acf(v))
  save_plot(v$id, "pacf", function() plot_pacf(v))
}

4 VAR estimation

Variables are split into endogenous/exogenous automatically from each variable’s role in config. Eleven monthly seasonal dummies (Feb-Dec; Jan is the reference month) are always appended to the exogenous block to control for calendar seasonality. The lag order follows config$lag_selection (fixed or auto via vars::VARselect()).

var_out <- estimate_var(model_data, config)
cat(sprintf("Lag order p = %d (method: %s). Estimation sample: %d observations.\n",
            var_out$p, config$lag_selection$method, nrow(var_out$endo) - var_out$p))
## Lag order p = 12 (method: fixed). Estimation sample: 239 observations.

5 Diagnostics

Per the thesis’s model-validation requirements: unit-root tests (ADF, KPSS), a Johansen cointegration test, VAR residual diagnostics (autocorrelation, normality), and companion-matrix stability. One compact table per check – read the statistics against the reported critical values / p-values directly, no automatic interpretation.

5.1 Deterministic components and unit roots

stationarity <- stationarity_table(raw_data, config)
knitr::kable(stationarity, digits = 3, caption = stationarity_note(stationarity))
Unit-root tests on deterministic-adjusted series. Every cell is the test statistic with its p-value in parentheses, and the two tests point in opposite directions: ADF H0 is a unit root, so p < 0.05 favours stationarity, while KPSS H0 is stationarity, so p < 0.05 favours a unit root. An I(1) series therefore shows adf_level not significant and kpss_level significant, with the _diff columns (the same two tests on the first difference) reversing both. Terms removed before testing, by row: pun = const; gas_price = const; energy_consumption = const + season; ipi = const + season – const is the regression intercept, trend a linear trend, season 11 centred monthly dummies (Feb-Dec, each minus 1/12). ADF uses type = trend where a trend was removed and type = drift otherwise, searching up to 12 augmentation lags by AIC; its p comes from MacKinnon’s response surface. KPSS uses type = mu at the short and long Newey-West bandwidths; its p is interpolated from tabulated critical values and so is bounded to [0.01, 0.10]. Zivot-Andrews is in the next table.

6 Identification

Structural shocks are identified via sign restrictions read generically from config$shocks – adding a shock or a restriction requires no changes to 05_sign_restrictions.R. For each of config$identification$n_draws Haar-uniform random rotations \(Q\), the structural impact matrix \(B_0 = P Q\) is checked against every configured shock’s sign restrictions; admissible draws are kept, and the Fry-Pagan median-target draw (the single admissible model closest to the pointwise median IRF) is reported, rather than the pointwise median itself.

Three shocks are labelled out of the \(K = 4\) available, so identification is partial throughout: an aggregate demand shock, a gas-specific shock, and an electricity supply shock specific to the Italian market. Their restriction sets are constructed to be pairwise disjoint, so that no admissible rotation can satisfy two of them in the same column of \(B_0\). This matters more than it may appear: when two labelled shocks share a region of the sign space, the same economic disturbance is assigned to different columns in different draws, and the pooled distribution of impulse responses mixes them – the labelling problem of Fry & Pagan (2011, sec. 4). Two margins do the separating.

The first is quantity. A disturbance that moves the electricity price and electricity consumption in the same direction is a shift of demand along an upward-sloping supply curve; one that moves them in opposite directions is a shift of supply along a downward-sloping demand curve. The sign of energy_consumption therefore separates the aggregate demand shock from the two contractionary shocks, and is the standard supply/demand identification argument (Kilian & Murphy, 2012).

The second is the relative price. Both contractionary shocks raise PUN, so the level of the electricity price cannot tell them apart; what does is the electricity-price response net of the gas-price response, \(\theta_{\text{pun}} - \theta_{\text{gas}}\) at impact. Under a gas-specific shock PUN rises because TTF rises, and pass-through in logs is less than one-for-one – PUN also embeds the CO\(_2\) price, non-fuel variable costs, and the hours in which gas is not the marginal technology – so the contrast is negative. An electricity supply shock (plant outages, hydrological shortfall, low renewable output, constrained imports) originates downstream of the gas market, and Italy is a price taker on TTF, so PUN rises while the gas price stays roughly flat and the contrast is positive. This is a restriction on log responses, an elasticity comparison, and not a spark spread measured in EUR/MWh; it restricts neither price level. A zero restriction on the gas response would state the price-taking argument more directly, but requires the mixed sign-and-zero algorithm of Arias, Rubio-Ramírez & Waggoner (2018) in place of the Haar-uniform rotations used here.

Industrial production is left unrestricted under the electricity supply shock. The macro cost of energy disturbances is the quantity this model is built to measure, and restricting the sign of ipi would assume a substantial part of that answer; the scales do not match either, since PUN is Italian while the industrial production index is EU-wide. It is retained under the gas-specific shock, where both the disturbance and the aggregate are European.

Finally, a sign normalisation: a positive realisation of the gas-specific or the electricity supply shock is an adverse disturbance, raising price and lowering quantity. Impulse responses and historical decomposition contributions below are to be read in that direction.

ident <- identify_sign_restrictions(var_out$fit, config)

cat(sprintf(
  "Acceptance rate: %.2f%% (%d / %d rotations admissible).\n",
  100 * ident$draws$acceptance_rate, ident$draws$n_accepted, ident$draws$n_draws
))
## Acceptance rate: 0.18% (549 / 300000 rotations admissible).

The acceptance rate is a diagnostic of how informative the restrictions are: a low rate means the restrictions rule out most of the rotation space (informative, but a non-refutability check worth keeping in mind); a rate near 100% means the restrictions barely bind.

restr_table <- purrr::map_dfr(config$shocks, function(s) {
  purrr::imap_dfr(s$restrictions, function(r, var_id) {
    tibble::tibble(shock = s$name, variable = var_id, sign = r$sign,
                    horizons = paste(range(r$horizons), collapse = ":"))
  })
})
knitr::kable(restr_table, caption = "Configured sign restrictions")

7 Bootstrap

Frequentist confidence bands (Inoue & Kilian, 2013): the reduced-form VAR residuals are resampled, the sample is rebuilt recursively, the VAR is re-estimated, and the entire identification search above is re-run inside every replication – not just a coefficient resample.

boot_out <- run_bootstrap(var_out$fit, var_out$endo, var_out$exo, var_out$p, config)

cat(sprintf(
  "Bootstrap: %d replications, %d succeeded, %d found no admissible rotation.\n",
  boot_out$n_boot, boot_out$n_ok, boot_out$n_failed
))
## Bootstrap: 2000 replications, 2000 succeeded, 0 found no admissible rotation.
cat(sprintf(
  "Mean acceptance rate across successful replications: %.2f%%.\n",
  100 * mean(boot_out$boot_acceptance_rates)
))
## Mean acceptance rate across successful replications: 0.19%.
theme_par(mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
h <- hist(100 * boot_out$boot_acceptance_rates, breaks = 15, plot = FALSE)
## Drawn twice so the grid sits behind the bars: plot.histogram() has no
## panel.first.
plot(h, col = NA, border = NA, main = "Bootstrap replications: acceptance rate distribution",
     xlab = "Acceptance rate (%)", ylab = "Replications")
grid_h()
plot(h, col = pal[["skyblue"]], border = "white", add = TRUE)

8 Results

Median-target impulse responses with 68% bootstrap confidence bands. Every endogenous variable enters the VAR in logs, so the responses are percent deviations from baseline to a one-standard-deviation structural shock (log points x 100; exactly, 100(e^theta - 1)).

plot_irf_grid <- function(mt_irf, bands, var_names, shock_names, var_labels) {
  n_shocks <- length(shock_names)
  n_vars <- length(var_names)
  h <- seq_len(dim(mt_irf)[3]) - 1

  ## Bottom margin 4, not 3: the last row carries the "Horizon (months)"
  ## label at mgp[1] = 2.4 lines, which a 3-line margin clips.
  old_par <- theme_par(mfrow = c(n_vars, n_shocks), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
  on.exit(par(old_par))

  for (v in seq_len(n_vars)) {
    for (s in seq_len(n_shocks)) {
      ## All endogenous variables enter the VAR in logs, so the responses are
      ## log points; x100 reads them as percent deviations from baseline.
      point <- 100 * mt_irf[v, s, ]
      lo <- 100 * bands$lower[v, s, ]
      hi <- 100 * bands$upper[v, s, ]

      plot(h, point, type = "n", ylim = range(c(point, lo, hi), na.rm = TRUE),
           xlab = if (v == n_vars) "Horizon (months)" else "",
           ylab = paste0(var_labels[v], " (%)"),
           main = if (v == 1) gsub("_", " ", shock_names[s]) else "",
           panel.first = grid_h())
      polygon(c(h, rev(h)), c(lo, rev(hi)),
              col = grDevices::adjustcolor(pal[["blue"]], alpha.f = 0.18), border = NA)
      abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey55")
      lines(h, point, col = pal[["blue"]], lwd = 2)
    }
  }
}

## config labels carry the RAW series' units ("PUN (EUR/MWh)"), which are wrong
## on an IRF axis: the responses are percent deviations, not levels. Strip the
## trailing unit parenthesis -- plot_irf_grid() appends "(%)" instead. Only the
## IRF grid uses these; the raw-series and ACF panels read v$label directly.
var_labels <- sub("\\s*\\(.*\\)$", "", purrr::map_chr(config$variables, "label"))
names(var_labels) <- purrr::map_chr(config$variables, "id")
plot_irf_grid(ident$mt$mt_irf, boot_out$bands, ident$var_names, ident$shock_names,
              var_labels[ident$var_names])

8.1 Variance decomposition

Share of each variable’s h-step forecast error variance attributable to the identified shocks, for the same Fry-Pagan median-target model as the impulse responses above. Horizons are months after impact, so h = 0 is the impact period. Identification is partial – only the shocks in config$shocks are pinned down – so the denominator is the full reduced-form forecast error variance implied by \(\Sigma_u\), not the sum over the identified columns of \(B_0\). The identified shares consequently sum to less than one, and the unidentified column is the remainder left to the shocks the sign restrictions do not identify. It is reported as-is: rescaling the shares to sum to one would claim an identification this design does not deliver.

Brackets are 68% pointwise percentile bands over the same pooled bootstrap draws as the IRF bands – the FEVD is computed inside each replication, so no second bootstrap pass is run.

fevd_mt <- fevd_median_target(var_out$fit, ident, config$identification$horizon)
fevd_names <- c(gsub("_", " ", ident$shock_names), "Unidentified")

fevd_tbl <- purrr::imap_dfr(config$fevd$horizons, function(h, k) {
  tbl <- tibble::tibble(horizon = h, variable = unname(var_labels[ident$var_names]))
  for (b in seq_along(fevd_names)) {
    tbl[[fevd_names[b]]] <- sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", fevd_mt[, b, h + 1],
                                     boot_out$fevd_bands$lower[, b, k],
                                     boot_out$fevd_bands$upper[, b, k])
  }
  tbl
})
knitr::kable(fevd_tbl, caption = paste0(
  "Forecast error variance decomposition, median-target model, with ",
  sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * config$bootstrap$conf_level), " bootstrap bands"))

#' Stacked-area FEVD, one panel per variable: the identified shocks' shares
#' stacked from the bottom and the unidentified remainder filling the gap up
#' to one, so how much of each variable the restrictions actually explain is
#' the visible grey band rather than something the reader has to subtract.
plot_fevd_grid <- function(fevd, band_names, var_labels) {
  h <- seq_len(dim(fevd)[3]) - 1
  n_vars <- dim(fevd)[1]
  cols <- c(unname(pal[c("blue", "orange", "bluishgreen", "reddishpurple")])[
    seq_len(length(band_names) - 1)], "grey85")

  old_par <- theme_par(mfrow = c(ceiling(n_vars / 2), 2), mar = c(3.5, 4, 3, 1),
                       oma = c(0, 0, 3, 0))
  on.exit(par(old_par))

  for (v in seq_len(n_vars)) {
    cum <- rbind(0, apply(fevd[v, , ], 2, cumsum))
    plot(h, cum[nrow(cum), ], type = "n", ylim = c(0, 1),
         xlab = if (v > n_vars - 2) "Horizon (months)" else "",
         ylab = "Share of forecast error variance",
         main = var_labels[v], panel.first = grid_h())
    for (b in seq_along(band_names)) {
      polygon(c(h, rev(h)), c(cum[b, ], rev(cum[b + 1, ])), col = cols[b], border = NA)
    }
  }
  top_legend(legend = band_names, fill = cols, ncol = 2)
}

plot_fevd_grid(fevd_mt, fevd_names, var_labels[ident$var_names])

8.2 Historical decomposition

Where the FEVD asks how much of the average forecast error each shock explains, the historical decomposition asks what each shock did in each individual month of the estimation sample. It uses the same Fry-Pagan median-target model as the impulse responses and the variance decomposition above: the structural shocks are recovered by inverting that single \(B_0\) through the reduced-form residuals (\(\varepsilon_t = B_0^{-1} u_t\)) and convolved with the structural moving-average weights \(\Theta_h = \Phi_h B_0\). Nothing is re-estimated and no rotation is redrawn.

Identification is partial here in exactly the sense it is in the FEVD. \(B_0\) is a full invertible \(K \times K\) matrix, so all \(K\) structural shocks are recoverable for this rotation, but only the shocks in config$shocks carry an economic label; the remaining columns are summed into a single other shocks band rather than rescaled away or dropped.

The baseline is everything the structural shocks do not move: the intercept, the 11 monthly seasonal dummies, the exogenous block (the energy_crisis dummy and res_capacity), and the effect of the \(p\) presample values. It is therefore not a pure trend – in particular the energy-crisis dummy’s effect sits in the baseline, so the gas shock is credited only with what that dummy leaves unexplained, and the 2022 bars should be read against a baseline that has already shifted. Contributions of all \(K\) shocks sum to the plotted deviation by construction, so the bars add up to the black line in every month.

No bootstrap bands and no per-episode contribution tables are reported for the historical decomposition: it is the point-estimate path of the median-target model.

hd <- historical_decomposition(var_out, ident)
cat(sprintf("Historical decomposition over %d months, %s to %s.\n",
            nrow(hd$y_dev), min(hd$dates), max(hd$dates)))
## Historical decomposition over 239 months, 2006-02-01 to 2025-12-01.
#' Stacked contribution bars over time, one panel per endogenous variable,
#' with the actual deviation from baseline drawn on top in black. barplot()
#' stacks mixed-sign columns wrong (every segment is laid out from zero
#' upward, so negative contributions overwrite positive ones), so the
#' contributions are split into their positive and negative parts and drawn
#' as two stacked barplots sharing one ylim; the segments then meet at zero
#' and their net total is the black line by construction.
plot_hd_grid <- function(hd, var_labels) {
  n_shocks <- length(hd$shock_names)
  n_vars <- dim(hd$contrib)[2]
  band_names <- c(gsub("_", " ", hd$shock_names), "Other Shocks")
  ## Same shock -> colour mapping as the FEVD panels, grey for the shocks
  ## the restrictions do not identify.
  cols <- c(unname(pal[c("blue", "orange", "bluishgreen", "reddishpurple")])[
    seq_len(n_shocks)], "grey85")
  at <- seq(1, length(hd$dates), by = 12)

  old_par <- theme_par(mfrow = c(n_vars, 1), mar = c(2.5, 4.5, 2.5, 1),
                       oma = c(0, 0, 3, 0))
  on.exit(par(old_par))

  for (v in seq_len(n_vars)) {
    ## All endogenous variables enter the VAR in logs, so x100 reads the
    ## contributions as percent deviations, exactly as in the IRF grid.
    m <- 100 * t(cbind(hd$contrib[, v, seq_len(n_shocks)],
                       rowSums(hd$contrib[, v, -seq_len(n_shocks), drop = FALSE])))
    pos <- pmax(m, 0)
    neg <- pmin(m, 0)

    ## Drawn empty first so the grid sits behind the bars (barplot() has no
    ## panel.first) and to take the bar midpoints from its return value.
    bp <- barplot(pos, space = 0, col = NA, border = NA,
                  ylim = range(colSums(pos), colSums(neg)),
                  ylab = "Percent deviation from baseline", main = var_labels[v])
    grid_h()
    barplot(pos, space = 0, col = cols, border = NA, add = TRUE, axes = FALSE)
    barplot(neg, space = 0, col = cols, border = NA, add = TRUE, axes = FALSE)
    abline(h = 0, col = "grey55")
    lines(bp, 100 * hd$y_dev[, v], col = "black", lwd = 1.2)
    axis(1, at = bp[at], labels = format(hd$dates[at], "%Y"))
  }
  top_legend(legend = c(band_names, "actual deviation"),
             fill = c(cols, NA), col = "black",
             lty = c(rep(NA, length(cols)), 1), lwd = c(rep(NA, length(cols)), 1.2),
             ncol = 3)
}

plot_hd_grid(hd, var_labels[ident$var_names])

8.3 Conditional forecast

The conditional forecasts hold the reduced form and the admissible rotations fixed at the 2006–2025 estimates above: nothing is re-estimated and no rotation is redrawn on the 2026 data. Every series is reloaded to cf$data_end with the same transformations; RES installed capacity, which has no 2026 values, is carried forward by its last monthly step. The one-step-ahead forecast error of month \(t\) uses the fixed coefficients and the realised lags, \(u_t = y_t - \hat y_{t|t-1}\), and the structural shocks are \(\varepsilon_t = B_0^{-1} u_t\), in standard deviations. A variable missing in the last data month is set to its expectation given that month’s observed errors, \(E[u_m \mid u_o] = \Sigma_{mo} \Sigma_{oo}^{-1} u_o\): a nowcast, not data.

Every forward path is the zero-residual forecast from the last data month plus the effect of an \(H \times K\) matrix \(W\) of future structural shocks, \(\sum_{s \le t} \Theta_{t-s} w_s\) – the historical decomposition’s convolution, run forward. Bands are 68% pointwise percentiles over the admissible rotations: they measure identification uncertainty alone, with the reduced form at its point estimate, and no bootstrap is run here.

cf_out <- conditional_forecast(var_out, ident, hd, config)
pct_cf <- sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * config$bootstrap$conf_level)
n_cf <- length(cf_out$dates)

cat(sprintf("Ex post: %s to %s. Forecast from %s: %s to %s (%d months).\n",
            format(min(cf_out$a_dates), "%b %Y"), format(max(cf_out$a_dates), "%b %Y"),
            format(cf_out$dates[n_cf], "%b %Y"), format(min(cf_out$fdates), "%b %Y"),
            format(max(cf_out$fdates), "%b %Y"), length(cf_out$fdates)))
## Ex post: Jan 2026 to Jul 2026. Forecast from Aug 2026: Sep 2026 to Dec 2027 (16 months).
if (length(cf_out$nowcast) > 0) {
  cat(sprintf("Nowcast, not data (%s): %s.\n", format(cf_out$dates[n_cf], "%b %Y"),
              paste(sprintf("%s = %.1f", cf_out$nowcast, exp(cf_out$y[n_cf, cf_out$nowcast])),
                    collapse = ", ")))
}
## Nowcast, not data (Aug 2026): ipi = 63.7.
cat(sprintf(paste("Checks, max abs error: one-step error vs VAR residual %.1e;",
                  "TTF vs target %.1e; reference path across rotations %.1e.\n"),
            cf_out$checks[[1]], cf_out$checks[[2]], cf_out$checks[[3]]))
## Checks, max abs error: one-step error vs VAR residual 1.7e-14; TTF vs target 1.5e-14; reference path across rotations 3.6e-15.

8.3.1 Ex post: the 2026 shocks

The one-step-ahead structural shocks of the months after the estimation sample in which all four variables are observed. The attack month (cf$attack_month) is set against March 2022 and against the distribution of \(|\varepsilon|\) over the estimation sample, both for the median-target model. Switching cf$attack_shocks off from the attack month on removes their contribution, \(\sum_{s \ge \text{attack}} \Theta_{t-s} \varepsilon_s\), from the data.

knitr::kable(cf_out$shock_table, digits = 0, caption = paste0(
  "One-step-ahead structural shocks (s.d.): median-target model, ", pct_cf,
  " band over admissible rotations in brackets. Percentile: share of estimation-sample ",
  "months with a smaller |shock|, median-target model."))

cf_cols <- stats::setNames(
  c(unname(pal[c("blue", "orange", "bluishgreen", "reddishpurple")])[seq_along(ident$shock_names)],
    "grey85"),
  cf_out$shock_names)

#' One path with its rotation band behind it.
band_line <- function(x, mid, lo, hi, col) {
  polygon(c(x, rev(x)), c(lo, rev(hi)),
          col = grDevices::adjustcolor(col, alpha.f = 0.18), border = NA)
  lines(x, mid, col = col, lwd = 2)
}

#' One panel per structural shock: the median-target one-step shock of each
#' ex-post month (bars, s.d.) with its rotation band (whiskers). The shaded
#' month is the attack month.
plot_cf_shocks <- function(cf, cols) {
  x <- seq_along(cf$a_dates)
  a <- match(cf$attack, cf$a_dates)
  old_par <- theme_par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(3, 4, 3, 1))
  on.exit(par(old_par))

  for (j in seq_along(cf$shock_names)) {
    plot(range(x) + c(-0.5, 0.5), range(0, cf$eps$lower[, j], cf$eps$upper[, j]),
         type = "n", xaxt = "n", xlab = "", ylab = "Shock (s.d.)",
         main = gsub("_", " ", cf$shock_names[j]),
         panel.first = {
           rect(a - 0.5, -1e6, a + 0.5, 1e6, col = "grey93", border = NA)
           grid_h()
         })
    rect(x - 0.35, 0, x + 0.35, cf$eps$mt[, j], col = cols[j], border = NA)
    arrows(x, cf$eps$lower[, j], x, cf$eps$upper[, j], angle = 90, code = 3,
           length = 0.03, col = "grey30")
    abline(h = 0, col = "grey55")
    axis(1, at = x, labels = format(cf$a_dates, "%b"))
  }
}

#' One forward panel: the reference path dashed and each of `readings` with
#' its rotation band, all from the origin month. PUN and TTF in EUR/MWh after
#' the observed months since Jan 2025; consumption and IPI in % (100 x log)
#' deviation from the reference path.
plot_cf_panel <- function(cf, v, readings, cols, main) {
  n <- length(cf$dates)
  xf <- c(cf$dates[n], cf$fdates)
  level <- v %in% c("pun", "gas_price")
  past <- level & cf$dates >= as.Date("2025-01-01")
  path <- function(q, r) {
    p <- q[, v, r]
    if (level) exp(c(cf$y[n, v], p)) else c(0, 100 * (p - cf$paths$mt[, v, "reference"]))
  }

  plot(range(cf$dates[past], xf),
       range(exp(cf$y[past, v]), path(cf$paths$mt, "reference"),
             sapply(readings, path, q = cf$paths$lower),
             sapply(readings, path, q = cf$paths$upper)),
       type = "n", xlab = "", ylab = if (level) "EUR/MWh" else "% deviation from reference",
       main = main, panel.first = grid_h())
  for (r in readings) {
    band_line(xf, path(cf$paths$mt, r), path(cf$paths$lower, r), path(cf$paths$upper, r),
              cols[[r]])
  }
  ## Explicit black: theme_par()'s `fg` also sets the default line colour.
  lines(xf, path(cf$paths$mt, "reference"), lty = 2, lwd = 1.5, col = "black")
  if (level) lines(cf$dates[past], exp(cf$y[past, v]), lwd = 1.5, col = "black")
}
plot_cf_shocks(cf_out, cf_cols)

cf_col <- cf_cols[[config$cf$attack_shocks[1]]]
theme_par(mar = c(3, 4.5, 3, 1), oma = c(0, 0, 3, 0))

       panel.first = grid_h())
  abline(v = cf_out$attack, lty = 2, col = "grey55")
  band_line(cf_out$a_dates, mt, lower, upper, cf_col)
  lines(cf_out$a_dates, actual, lwd = 2, col = "black")
})

           lwd = 2, ncol = 2)

  " band over admissible rotations in brackets."))

8.3.2 Persistence (D1)

TTF is held at its last observed level to cf$horizon_end, and the gap \(r_t\) between that target and the zero-residual forecast is closed three ways. With all shocks free, the minimum-norm shocks \(w = R'(RR')^{-1} r\) (Waggoner & Zha, 1999), where \(R\) collects \(\Theta_{t-s}[\text{TTF}, j]\) over months \(s \le t\) and shocks \(j\), give the reference path: the path is the same under every admissible rotation, the implied shocks are not. With one shock alone – gas-specific, or industrial demand – the shocks solve a lower-triangular system month by month, every other shock at zero. That system divides by the impact response of TTF to the shock, which the sign restriction bounds only at zero; in the admissible rotations where it is nearly zero the implied shocks explode, so a single-shock reading enters its band only in the rotations where it is numerically defined (TTF on the target and every path finite). PUN and TTF are in EUR/MWh; consumption and IPI in percent (100 x log) deviation from the reference path.

cat(sprintf(paste("Single-shock readings numerically defined in %d (gas-specific) and %d",
                  "(industrial demand) of %d admissible rotations.\n"),
            cf_out$n_defined[["gas"]], cf_out$n_defined[["demand"]], cf_out$n_rotations))
## Single-shock readings numerically defined in 524 (gas-specific) and 528 (industrial demand) of 549 admissible rotations.
d1_cols <- c(gas = cf_cols[["Gas-Specific_Shock"]], demand = cf_cols[["Industrial_Demand_Shock"]])
theme_par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(3, 4.5, 3, 1), oma = c(0, 0, 3, 0))
for (v in c("pun", "gas_price", "energy_consumption", "ipi")) {
  plot_cf_panel(cf_out, v, names(d1_cols), d1_cols, var_labels[[v]])
}
top_legend(legend = c("observed", "reference (all shocks)", "gas-specific only",
                      "industrial demand only"),
           col = c("black", "black", d1_cols), lty = c(1, 2, 1, 1), lwd = c(1.5, 1.5, 2, 2),
           ncol = 4)

8.3.3 Escalation stress test (C1) and comparison

C1 replays the median-target gas-specific shocks of cf$c1_window, from the month after the origin and with every other shock at zero, on top of the reference path; in the band, each rotation replays its own shocks of that window. The table compares the four forward paths.

c1_col <- c(c1 = cf_cols[["Gas-Specific_Shock"]])
theme_par(mar = c(3, 4.5, 3, 1), oma = c(0, 0, 3, 0))
plot_cf_panel(cf_out, "pun", "c1", c1_col, "PUN: escalation stress test (C1)")
top_legend(legend = c("observed", "reference (all shocks)", "escalation (C1)"),
           col = c("black", "black", c1_col), lty = c(1, 2, 1), lwd = c(1.5, 1.5, 2), ncol = 3)

  " band over admissible rotations in brackets (none where every rotation agrees). ",
  "PUN in EUR/MWh; IPI and consumption in % (100 x log) deviation from the reference path in ",
  format(max(cf_out$fdates), "%b %Y"), "; peak month of the median-target path."))
